sections.title: Personal projects
sections.intro: Two apps I built for managing finances and reusing clipboard history.

items.title: Finance Studio
items.subtitle: AI Integrated Web and Mobile Finance App
items.summary: Track transactions, investments, and savings goals across personal and small-business finances.

image.alt: Finance Studio overview with fictional balances and cash-flow charts
image.caption: Live demo · Fictional data

blocks.heading: Shared financial model
paragraphs: I built a Next.js web app and a native React Native companion with Expo. Both use Supabase Auth and the same PostgreSQL schema, so a user can sign in on either platform and access the same finance sheets. PostgreSQL row-level policies restrict users to their own records.

I ported the ledger calculations and validation to mobile so transfers, split reimbursements, investment valuations, and savings goals follow the same rules. Reporting keeps totals separate by currency and uses Asia/Jakarta dates for period boundaries.

blocks.heading: AI-assisted entry on the web
paragraphs: The web assistant uses server-side Gemini tool calls to turn natural-language instructions and PDF statements into editable transaction drafts. The app validates the proposed fields, flags possible duplicates, and compares extracted statement totals with the draft rows before the user reviews and submits them.
The public AI demo uses a fixed fictional workspace. The mobile assistant uses a local English and Indonesian parser for draft entry and follow-up corrections.

blocks.heading: Mobile sync and conflict handling
paragraphs: I designed the mobile data layer for people who switch between their phone and browser. Mobile updates and deletes match the version originally opened, so a newer database change can surface as a conflict while the mobile draft stays open. A serialized write queue and stable IDs for new entries prevent overlapping saves and help retries avoid duplicate records.

Refreshes triggered by app foregrounding, reconnects, and available Realtime events share an active request. The app retains the last loaded view if a refresh fails. Demo records stay in local storage, and authentication sessions use Expo SecureStore on native devices.

blocks.heading: Reports and verification
paragraphs: The web app generates PDF statements for cash activity, reimbursements, and investments. The mobile companion exports A4 reports through the native share sheet. Transaction filters narrow the line items while the running balances still reflect the full reporting period.
Automated tests cover ledger calculations, stale edits and retries, session storage, and statement output.

items.title: SnipMoor
items.subtitle: Windows clipboard manager
items.summary: Save, search, and reuse clipboard entries with a global keyboard shortcut.

image.alt: SnipMoor’s compact Windows clipboard history panel with fictional example clips
image.caption: App preview · Sample clips

blocks.heading: Windows clipboard integration
paragraphs: I built the React interface in Tauri and used Rust for the Windows clipboard integration. A configurable global shortcut opens a compact picker from the current application. Users can search their history and paste several text clips together or reuse a single screenshot.
I kept clipboard capture opt-in and added capture pause and app exclusions so users can control what enters their history.

blocks.heading: Search and on-device OCR
paragraphs: SnipMoor indexes clip text, titles, tags, source apps, and recognized screenshot text with SQLite FTS5. Screenshots go through the Windows OCR engine on the device, so they can be searched by the words they contain.
The same library supports saved snippets, tags, expiry, and recoverable trash, so frequently used material can be organized alongside recent clips.

blocks.heading: Encrypted storage and backups
paragraphs: The local library uses SQLCipher, with Windows-protected keys. Portable encrypted backups let users move their library while preserving its privacy.

blocks.heading: Licensing and desktop releases
paragraphs: I built a separate Cloudflare Workers and D1 service for device-bound licensing and activation. The desktop client verifies signed access grants and can continue to operate offline for a limited period.

I set up a signed Tauri update flow. The release tooling produces the installer, updater signature, update manifest, and checksums. Tests cover the native clipboard and licensing service alongside browser tests for the interface.

sections.title: Research & Publications
sections.intro: My research on making Indonesian Sign Language (BISINDO) recognition practical on devices with limited computing power.

items.title: Hybrid MediaPipe-GRU Architecture for Efficient BISINDO Recognition Integrating Non-Manual Markers in Low-Resource Environments
items.subtitle: Under review · JOIV
items.authors: Muhammad Anang Ayman Ramadhana, Nicholas Ho, Jason Luman, Rhio Sutoyo
items.summary: We propose a lightweight model that recognizes BISINDO signs using hand movements, body pose, and facial cues. It is designed to run offline on devices with limited resources.

blocks.heading: Recognizing signs and facial cues
paragraphs: We use MediaPipe to extract hand, pose, and facial landmarks from video. A gated recurrent unit (GRU) network uses those sequences to classify isolated signs across a vocabulary of 40 BISINDO words.

blocks.heading: Designing for offline use
paragraphs: The approach uses landmark coordinates as model inputs and targets on-device inference. The evaluation plan covers classification performance, model size, and inference latency on hardware with limited resources.

items.title: Multimodal Skeletal and Facial Landmark Dataset for Indonesian Sign Language (BISINDO) Non-Manual Marker Recognition
items.subtitle: Under review · Data in Brief
items.authors: Jason Luman, Muhammad Anang Ayman Ramadhana, Nicholas Ho, Rhio Sutoyo
items.summary: We extracted hand, pose, and facial landmarks from 2,400 BISINDO videos covering 40 words. The dataset supports research on recognizing both hand gestures and facial cues.

blocks.heading: Vocabulary and capture
paragraphs: The dataset contains 60 recordings for each of 40 words. Twenty words emphasize non-manual signals such as facial expressions, and twenty represent standard manual signs. We recorded with consumer webcams in everyday lighting and backgrounds.

blocks.heading: Data format
paragraphs: Each sample uses 149 three-dimensional landmarks per frame: 33 for pose, 42 for the hands, and 74 for the face. We normalized the coordinates relative to the shoulders and standardized each sequence to 30 frames. The processed samples are available as NumPy arrays on Mendeley Data.
